Chapter 2: Entering the Amish World—New Rules, Old Fears
When a chance came to leave their old life behind, it didn’t exactly look like freedom. It showed up as a strict religious community—a place that seemed to promise safety, order, and maybe even a sense of belonging. Their mother, searching for a fresh start or maybe just a new way to keep control, brought the girls right into the heart of Amish life.
At first, everything was overwhelming. Imagine stepping into a world where almost everything you know is suddenly different. The Amish community had rules for everything—how you dress, how you speak, even how you work. The clothes were plain, and every day revolved around chores and prayer. There was no electricity, no TV, and the only music came from old hymns. The girls had to learn to wake up before dawn, milk cows, scrub floors, and even bake bread from scratch.
For some folks, living this way feels peaceful and grounding. But for these girls, it turned out to be just another kind of prison. The community was tight-knit, but outsiders? They were always watched with a bit of suspicion. The girls, with their different ways and awkwardness, stood out no matter how hard they tried. They did their best to blend in—to learn the dialect, to follow every rule. But you can probably guess, mistakes happened. And when they did, the consequences came quickly.
Their mother’s grip didn’t loosen in this new world. If anything, it got even stronger. She used the community’s strictness as yet another tool, telling the girls that if they disobeyed, they’d bring shame not just on themselves, but on the whole family. Questioning the rules? That was a sin. Suffering was just a test of faith.
The older sister, now a teenager, really felt the pressure. She wanted to believe this community could keep her safe, but those old fears just wouldn’t let go. The abuse at home kept happening, hidden behind a mask of religious devotion. Her mother’s new partner—her stepfather—fit right in. The community accepted him, ignoring or excusing his past. The girls were told to forgive, to pray, and to just endure.
School was different here, too. Education stopped at eighth grade, and the focus was always on practical things—cooking, sewing, farming. The older sister missed having the chance to learn more, to dream about a life beyond the tight boundaries of the community. She watched other girls get ready for marriage, their futures already decided for them.
The feeling of isolation only grew. In such a closed-off world, secrets were easy to keep. When the older sister tried to talk about the abuse, nobody really listened. Some people didn’t believe her. Others just stayed silent. The leaders told her to pray harder, to forgive, not to bring shame on her family by speaking up.
Eventually, it became painfully clear—the rules were there to protect the community, not the individual. The older sister felt completely trapped, stuck between her fear of her mother and stepfather, and the endless pressure to fit in. All she wanted was for someone to believe her, to see the reality hidden behind those plain dresses and quiet prayers.
And yet, even in all that darkness, she managed to find tiny moments of comfort. A kind neighbor might offer a gentle smile or a quiet word. The fields at sunrise, the slow rhythm of the seasons, the satisfaction of baking a perfect loaf of bread—these little things reminded her that life could be more than just pain.
Still, the fear never really disappeared. The past was always close by, and the future? Well, it felt more uncertain than ever.
